analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, effective roughly three months after enactment.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and saw no further action before Congress ended, drawing zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Living Wage Now Act would rewrite the federal minimum wage in the Fair Labor Standards Act, replacing the current $7.25-an-hour floor with a flat $15-an-hour requirement. The increase would take effect on the first day of the third month after the bill became law — a single step up, not a phased schedule of yearly raises. Introduced by Rep. Steve Cohen (D-TN) in January 2023, it was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers currently paid between $7.25 and $15 an hour, most of them in retail, food service, hospitality, and other labor-intensive service jobs, would see their hourly pay rise to the new floor. Workers earning slightly above $15 could also see raises if employers keep pay ladders intact.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the federal minimum wage at $15 an hour, replacing the $7.25 floor in effect since 2009, effective the first day of the third month after enactment.
The increase applies through the Fair Labor Standards Act's general minimum wage provision, which covers most employees engaged in interstate commerce or employed by covered enterprises.
The effective date is immediate rather than phased over several years, so affected workers would reach the full $15 within roughly three months of enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with substantial numbers of sub-$15 workers — restaurants, retailers, hotels, farms, and other labor-intensive businesses — would bear higher direct wage bills, and some of that cost could pass through to consumers as higher prices. Small businesses and employers in lower-wage regions would feel the squeeze sooner than under a phased-in increase.

drawbacks.text: The bill jumps from $7.25 to $15 in a single step about three months after enactment, with no multi-year phase-in, which critics of similar proposals warn could strain small businesses' payrolls quickly and force abrupt price increases or staffing cuts.

A uniform national $15 floor means the same wage requirement applies in low-cost regions and high-cost regions alike; an honest supporter acknowledges employers in low-wage labor markets absorb a larger relative increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: tens of millions of workers paid below $15 an hour would get a raise, and the current federal floor of $7.25 has lost substantial purchasing power since 2009. The main cost is a faster adjustment than a phased-in increase would allow, concentrated on labor-intensive employers and small businesses in low-wage areas, which could mean some job cuts or price increases during the transition. Whether the job losses outweigh the wage gains is contested in economics; what is not contested is that the bill gives a one-time boost to the lowest-paid workers and asks employers of low-wage labor to pay for it.

outcome.mechanism: It went straight to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there until the 118th Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Living Wage Now Act on January 25, 2023, proposing a $15 federal minimum wage.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; no further steps appear in its action history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over the full two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying below $15 an hour keep the current $7.25 federal floor, and the House majority is better off in the sense that a bill it did not bring to the floor never became law. The roughly 25 million workers in the United States who would have gained from a $15 federal minimum wage, by widely reported estimates of who earns under $15, are the ones who lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers paying under $15 keep the $7.25 floor

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Education and Workforce Committee.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 25, 2023 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the committee schedule and the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the House floor or act on it in committee during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill, no Republican or additional Democratic members signed on as cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committee and House majority never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would raise their wage floor from $7.25 to $15, directly increasing payroll costs for businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage workers. Their interest in stopping the bill ran against the wage gains the bill offered low-paid workers.

industries.industry: Labor-intensive agriculture and small businesses in low-wage regions
industries.note: A flat, unphased $15 floor raises their wage costs within about three months of enactment, with no regional adjustment. Their stake in the bill's failure was keeping the current lower wage floor.
